strengths: The paper identifies a real and useful problem: under heavy occlusion, image-to-3D generation is genuinely ambiguous, and allowing text or reference priors to steer the unseen regions is a meaningful task formulation.

RelaxFlow is a plausible and practical training-free framework. The dual-branch design, early semantic guidance schedule, visibility-aware fusion, and multi-prior conditioning are well motivated and appear compatible with existing rectified-flow 3D generators such as SAM3D and TRELLIS.

The experiments show consistent gains over the chosen backbones on ExtremeOcc-3D, especially for SAM3D: CLIP-text, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID all improve, suggesting the method can improve semantic steering without completely sacrificing observed-view fidelity.

The paper includes helpful ablations for low-pass relaxation, geometry masking, cutoff schedule, smoothing strength, number of priors, and generated versus retrieved priors. The qualitative figures also communicate the intended behavior clearly.
The limitations section honestly notes an important failure mode: when observation and prior conflict, the method may interpolate rather than satisfy either condition.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are much stronger than what is actually established. The key error-reduction result assumes the desired semantic signal is low-frequency and the model error is high-frequency, which is essentially the condition under which Gaussian smoothing helps. The link from attention-logit smoothing to low-pass filtering of the actual generative vector field is only supported by an additional Lipschitz assumption, so the proof does not convincingly justify the central mechanism beyond restating its intended effect.

The method is less directly text-driven than the title and framing suggest. Text is converted into retrieved or generated prior images, so performance depends heavily on external retrieval pools or a text-to-image model. This shifts part of the semantic disambiguation problem outside the proposed method and weakens claims about free-form language control.

The evaluation is promising but not yet fully convincing. ExtremeOcc-3D has 264 cases and AmbiSem-3D only 21 ambiguous cases; the latter relies largely on CLIP scores and a small user study. There is no strong geometry-level evaluation of visible-region preservation or occluded-region plausibility, despite the paper’s central claim of strict observation preservation plus semantically correct 3D completion.

Several metrics are imperfect for the claims. Minimum LPIPS over predicted views can overstate observation fidelity, CLIP scores are weak evidence for 3D semantic correctness, FID/Point-FID are distributional and may be unstable on small benchmarks, and the paper explicitly avoids stricter geometric errors without replacing them with a convincing task-specific alternative.

Baseline coverage and fairness leave questions. The compared systems are not all designed for text-plus-image amodal control, and some baselines receive prior images in relatively naive ways. Stronger simple baselines, such as direct prior/observation velocity interpolation without multi-prior consensus, alternative attention smoothing placements, or optimization-based text-image 3D editing under matched budgets, would clarify what is genuinely contributed by each component.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives many implementation details and hyperparameters, but does not specify code release, exact benchmark release procedure, random seeds, prior image samples/prompts, user-study interface/protocol details, or compute/runtime measurements beyond a qualitative statement of negligible overhead.

Presentation is generally understandable but has numerous typos and formatting issues, and some terminology such as semantic corridors, hard/soft forces, and strict preservation is more rhetorical than operationally defined. The paper would benefit from tightening these claims and separating empirical observations from theoretical guarantees.

Ethical and societal considerations are minimal. The work depends on external generative priors and 3D datasets, but does not discuss dataset licensing, potential bias inherited from text-to-image priors, or risks of generating misleading reconstructions from ambiguous/occluded evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: under heavy occlusion, image-to-3D generation is genuinely ambiguous, and text-conditioned amodal completion is a useful task formulation for robotics, AR/VR, and asset creation.

The proposed RelaxFlow framework has an intuitive modular structure: an observation branch preserves visible evidence, while a prior branch uses text-derived visual proxies, low-pass attention smoothing, and visibility-aware fusion to steer occluded regions.
The paper includes two diagnostic benchmarks and evaluates on two backbones, TRELLIS and SAM3D. The qualitative examples are helpful and make the intended behavior of the method clear.
The training-free nature of the method is practically attractive if the method proves robust, since it can be plugged into existing feedforward 3D generators without additional model training.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are not convincing. The claimed strict reduction in semantic estimation error relies on strong assumptions that the true semantic field is low-frequency and the model error is high-frequency, which are essentially the desired conclusion rather than empirically justified properties. The connection from cross-attention logit smoothing to low-pass filtering of the actual generative vector field is also only assumed through a Lipschitz condition and does not establish that the implemented operation has the claimed semantic effect.

The evaluation is too weak to support the broad claims. ExtremeOcc-3D has only 264 test cases and AmbiSem-3D has only 21 manually curated cases, so the benchmarks are small and potentially highly selected. The main automatic metrics, including CLIP scores, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID, are at best indirect proxies for text-guided amodal correctness and do not reliably measure whether the hidden geometry is semantically correct and observation-consistent.

The AmbiSem-3D user study is under-specified. The paper reports strong preference numbers from 32 volunteers but does not provide enough detail about randomization, interface, rater expertise, inter-rater agreement, statistical significance, or whether raters saw method identities/artifacts. Given that this is the most direct evidence for the ambiguous multi-solution setting, this omission is important.

The baselines are not sufficiently comprehensive or clearly fair. The paper compares mostly to image-to-3D backbones and 2D-edit-then-3D pipelines, but does not convincingly compare against strong text/image-conditioned 3D generation or editing alternatives with comparable conditioning. It is also unclear whether all baselines receive equally useful priors and whether they are tuned as carefully as the proposed method.

Several ablations are shallow. The reported drops from removing low-pass relaxation or the visibility mask are modest, and the paper does not isolate the effects of multi-prior consensus, prior source quality, retrieval versus generated priors, schedule choices, backbone-specific behavior, and prompt sensitivity in a way that makes the mechanism compelling.

The method may depend heavily on dataset-specific conveniences. For ExtremeOcc-3D, priors are sampled from the same category in the same dataset family, which may make the prior unusually well aligned with the evaluation distribution. It is not clear that the approach generalizes to open-vocabulary prompts, real photographs, non-furniture objects, unusual camera poses, or cases where the prompt and visible evidence are only partially compatible.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some hyperparameters, but important details about benchmark construction, prompt generation, prior image generation, exact backbone versions, solver settings, selection/filtering criteria, user-study protocol, and release plans are insufficient for independent replication and auditing.

The limitations and ethics discussion is too thin. A method that steers unseen 3D structure from text can hallucinate plausible but wrong geometry, and the paper does not adequately analyze failure modes, uncertainty, prompt bias, misuse risks, or how users should detect when generated hidden structure is unsupported by evidence.

Presentation is generally readable but not polished. There are typos and awkward phrasing, and some equations use inconsistent notation, for example switching between conditions and trajectories in ways that make the proofs harder to trust. The paper also overstates the strength of its theoretical and empirical evidence.

Originality is moderate at best. Combining visual priors, attention smoothing, dual-branch guidance, and visibility-based fusion is a reasonable engineering idea, but the individual ingredients are close to existing guidance, editing, and amodal completion techniques. The submission would need much stronger validation to justify acceptance as a substantial ICML contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important problem: under heavy occlusion, image-to-3D generation is semantically underdetermined, and text can be a natural way to specify the intended amodal completion. This task framing is useful and well motivated by concrete failure cases of feedforward models collapsing to a single observation-overfitted interpretation.

RelaxFlow is technically appealing as a training-free plug-in for existing feedforward 3D generators. The dual-branch design cleanly separates strict observation preservation from relaxed semantic guidance, and the visibility-aware fusion is well aligned with the problem structure.

The experiments are convincing overall. The method improves both TRELLIS and SAM3D on ExtremeOcc-3D, with particularly meaningful gains for SAM3D in CLIP-text alignment, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID. The AmbiSem-3D user study also shows a large preference margin for the proposed method over baselines.

The ablations support the main design choices: removing low-pass relaxation or the geometry visibility mask degrades performance, and the analysis of prior count, cutoff, smoothing strength, and generated versus retrieved priors helps characterize when the method works.

The paper is mostly clear and well organized. The pipeline, task setting, benchmark construction, and metric definitions are described in enough detail to understand the method and reproduce the evaluation at a high level.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are helpful for intuition but rest on strong and largely unvalidated assumptions: that semantic intent is low-frequency, that estimation errors are high-frequency, and that attention-logit smoothing induces the desired low-pass filtering of the generative vector field. The analysis does not by itself establish that these assumptions hold for the actual transformer backbones.

The evaluation benchmarks are useful but limited in scale and breadth. ExtremeOcc-3D has 264 cases and AmbiSem-3D only 21 ambiguous cases, so the evidence for broad generalization across object categories, scenes, and real-world occlusions remains incomplete.

The method is described as text-driven, but the implementation depends on converting text into visual priors via retrieval or a text-to-image model. This introduces a dependency on prior quality and makes it somewhat unclear how much of the gain comes from RelaxFlow versus from strong visual proxy construction.

Some baselines are not fully satisfying for the proposed setting. The comparisons include reasonable feedforward and edit-then-3D pipelines, but stronger or more carefully adapted multi-condition/text-guided 3D baselines would make the empirical case more decisive.

Reproducibility is adequate at the conceptual level but not complete from the manuscript alone. Important implementation details such as exact backbone versions, prior generation settings, user study protocol, and benchmark release/code availability are not sufficiently specified to ensure others can exactly reproduce the results.

The limitations discussion is honest but narrow. It notes failures under incompatible observation and prior conditions, but says little about ethical issues or practical risks from text-guided 3D asset generation, dataset biases inherited from 3D-FUTURE/ObjaverseXL/text-to-image priors, or possible misuse in synthetic content creation.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored problem: single-image 3D generation under severe occlusion is inherently ambiguous, and text/user intent is a natural way to choose among plausible amodal completions.

RelaxFlow is a practical training-free framework that can be attached to two different feedforward 3D backbones, with a clear decomposition into observation preservation, semantic-prior guidance, low-pass relaxation, and visibility-aware fusion.

The empirical results are promising: on ExtremeOcc-3D the SAM3D-based version improves CLIPimg, CLIPtxt, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID over SAM3D, and the ablations show that both low-pass relaxation and the visibility mask contribute to performance.

The paper includes useful diagnostic benchmarks for two complementary settings: extreme occlusion with ground-truth 3D assets, and semantic branching where multiple text-conditioned completions are plausible.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful pipeline figures, qualitative comparisons, implementation details, metric definitions, runtime measurements, and an explicit failure-case discussion.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are substantially stronger than what is justified. The low-frequency semantic/high-frequency error separation is assumed rather than demonstrated, and the claimed strict error reduction follows from assumptions that already encode the desired outcome. The connection from attention-logit smoothing to low-pass filtering of the actual generative vector field is only a Lipschitz-style plausibility argument, not a strong guarantee.

The evaluation relies heavily on proxy metrics such as CLIP, LPIPS, FID, and Point-FID, which are imperfect for judging whether the visible evidence is strictly preserved and whether 3D geometry is physically correct. There are no direct geometric error metrics on visible/occluded regions for the ExtremeOcc-3D cases where ground truth exists.

AmbiSem-3D is quite small in its main form, with only 21 manually designed cases. The 100-case extension helps, but is only compared against SAM3D and uses limited metrics, so the evidence for broad semantic-branching generalization remains incomplete.

The user study reports large preference margins, but the manuscript gives insufficient detail about randomization, interface, rater expertise, question wording, inter-rater agreement, or statistical significance. This makes the subjective evidence harder to assess.

The prior-image setup may make the task easier than a realistic text-only setting, especially on ExtremeOcc-3D where priors are retrieved from the same category pool as the benchmark source. The method depends on external generated/retrieved visual priors, so the text-driven framing is somewhat indirect.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and dataset curation are described, but there is no clear code/data release statement, no seed or variance reporting, limited details on baseline tuning, and reliance on recent or external systems may make exact reproduction difficult.

The method increases inference time substantially, about 1.8x to 2.5x depending on the backbone. The paper reports this honestly, but the practical tradeoff is important for feedforward 3D generation use cases.

The impact/ethics discussion is brief and generic; it acknowledges synthetic-content misuse and model/data bias but does not discuss mitigation, dataset licensing/consent issues for generated priors, or potential misuse specific to controllable 3D asset generation.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: under severe occlusion, image-to-3D generation is genuinely underdetermined and text can be useful for disambiguating unseen structure.
The proposed system is practical in spirit: it is training-free, plugs into SAM3D/TRELLIS, and combines text-derived visual priors with observation-preserving branches and visibility-aware fusion.

The manuscript includes several useful diagnostic components, including ExtremeOcc-3D, AmbiSem-3D, ablations for low-pass relaxation/visibility masking/prior count, runtime reporting, and a brief failure-case discussion.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not convincing. The low-pass analysis assumes, rather than demonstrates, that semantic intent is low-frequency and errors are high-frequency; the claimed equivalence between attention-logit blurring and low-pass filtering of the generative vector field is only supported by a Lipschitz-style assumption, not a proof tied to the actual transformer dynamics. As a result, the theory does not materially validate the method.

The evaluation is too weak to support the paper’s strong claims. ExtremeOcc-3D uses category-level priors and retrieved same-category objects from the source dataset, which risks making the task much easier than real text-driven amodal generation. AmbiSem-3D has only 21 manually curated cases in the main evaluation, and the 100-case extension reports only CLIP metrics against SAM3D.

The metrics are mostly proxy measures and do not directly establish correct amodal 3D completion. CLIP image/text scores, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID can miss geometric correctness, visible-surface preservation, and prompt-specific structural validity. The paper explicitly avoids strict geometry errors but does not replace them with a reliable task-specific alternative.

The user study is underdescribed. It reports very large preferences from 32 volunteers, but the manuscript does not provide enough detail on study design, randomization, interface, statistical uncertainty, annotation instructions, or whether evaluators saw method identities. This makes the strongest AmbiSem evidence difficult to trust.

Baseline fairness is questionable. Several baselines appear to be pipelines not designed for the task, while the proposed method receives carefully constructed prior images and task-specific fusion. The direct text+image and editing baselines are not analyzed deeply enough to show that the gain comes from the proposed relaxation rather than from stronger prior-image conditioning or hand-tuned fusion.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The method combines known ingredients: visual proxy priors, dual-branch guidance, attention smoothing, time-varying guidance, and visibility-aware blending. The new task framing is useful, but the algorithmic contribution feels incremental without stronger empirical validation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Some hyperparameters and dataset construction details are given, but the paper does not clearly commit to releasing code, generated/retrieved priors, benchmark splits, user-study materials, or exact inference settings needed to reproduce the results.

The limitations and ethics discussion are superficial. The paper notes conflicting-condition failures and generic misuse risks, but does not adequately discuss benchmark bias, dependence on proprietary or future models, generated-prior bias, ambiguity in ground truth, or the risk of fabricating plausible but incorrect 3D assets.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important gap in image-to-3D generation: under heavy occlusion, visible evidence can be insufficient, so text intent is genuinely needed to select among multiple plausible amodal completions.

RelaxFlow is a practical, training-free method that cleanly decomposes observation preservation and semantic guidance. The use of multi-prior visual proxies, low-pass attention-logit smoothing, and visibility-aware fusion is well motivated and appears compatible with existing feedforward 3D backbones.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. Results are reported on two backbones, TRELLIS and SAM3D, with comparisons to occlusion-aware models, 2D-edit-then-3D pipelines, video/multiview generation routes, commercial editing, and direct text+image fusion baselines.

The quantitative gains are meaningful, especially on ExtremeOcc-3D where RelaxFlow improves CLIP text alignment, FID, LPIPS, and Point-FID while also maintaining or improving observation alignment. The AmbiSem-3D user study shows a large preference for the proposed method.
The paper contributes useful diagnostic benchmarks, ExtremeOcc-3D and AmbiSem-3D, which target a real failure mode of current systems rather than only standard reconstruction fidelity.

The presentation is generally clear, with helpful qualitative examples, ablations, metric definitions, dataset curation details, runtime measurements, and an impact statement acknowledging misuse and bias risks.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is more explanatory than conclusive. Its key claims depend on strong assumptions, especially that semantic intent is low-frequency and estimator error is high-frequency, and these assumptions are not empirically validated in the actual model dynamics.
AmbiSem-3D is small in its main form, with only 21 curated cases. The 100-case extension helps, but the main user study and qualitative claims still lean heavily on a compact diagnostic set.

Several metrics are proxy measures whose limitations matter here. CLIP similarities, FID over rendered views, and Point-FID may not fully capture 3D geometric correctness, amodal consistency, or visible-region preservation under ambiguous completions.

The user study is useful but under-specified: the manuscript reports 32 volunteers and preference rates, but gives limited detail on randomization, interface, statistical confidence, inter-rater agreement, or whether annotators were blinded to methods.

The method depends on the quality and compatibility of prior images, either retrieved or generated. The paper includes a prior-source ablation, but failures under bad, biased, or subtly mismatched priors remain a material limitation.

Reproducibility would be stronger with explicit release commitments for code, benchmark splits, prompts, prior images, generation settings, random seeds, and model/version details. The manuscript provides many implementation details, but not enough to guarantee independent replication from the text alone.

The limitations discussion is relatively brief. It acknowledges conflicting observation-prior cases and general generative misuse/bias, but could more directly discuss benchmark coverage, prior dependence, runtime overhead, and possible failure modes in safety-critical 3D applications.
